title: United Nations Human Rights Council 61st Session . CIRAC Side Event Human Rights in South Asia: Historical State of Jammu and Kashmir Remains Forcibly Divided
excerpt: A high-level UN Human Rights Council side event examined the ongoing human rights crisis in South Asia and in the forcibly divided historical State of Jammu and Kashmir.
summary: A comprehensive account of the HRC61 side event highlighting human rights violations, political repression, demographic changes, and the urgent need for international accountability in the historical State of Jammu and Kashmir.
author: The Mirror Jammu Kashmir – Geneva Desk

heroImage.caption: HRC61 Side Event – Human Rights in South Asia, Palais des Nations, Geneva

body.text: UN Human Rights Council – 61st Session, Geneva

A high-level side event titled “Human Rights in South Asia, with a Special Focus on the Historical State of Jammu and Kashmir” was convened by the Comité International pour le Respect et l'Application de la Charte Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples (CIRAC) during the 61st Session of the United Nations Human Rights Council at Room XI, Palais des Nations, Geneva.
“The historical State of Jammu and Kashmir remains forcibly divided, and its people continue to face systemic human rights challenges.”

The event brought together prominent human rights defenders, political representatives, legal experts, and civil society actors to examine the evolving human rights situation in South Asia, with particular focus on the historical State of Jammu and Kashmir.
Background & Context

Among distinguished participants were member state delegates, human rights watchdogs, press and media, and rights activists including Sardar Amjad Yousaf, Sardar Tariq Khan, Tika Khan Tahir, Asif Abbas, Raja Sarfraz Khan, Sajid Hussain, Aqeel Ahmed, Abdul Shafiq Habegger, Syed Shafiq Ur Rehman, Muhammad Ziaul Mustafa, Syed Taqdees Ali Gillani, Syed Faisal Abbas Bukhari, Muhammad Ashfaq Abbasi, renowned journalist Muhammad Younas Khan, and others.
“Human rights concerns in South Asia cannot be isolated from the unresolved question of Jammu and Kashmir.”
SPEAKER: Anselme Mavula — Opening Remarks

body.caption: Anselme Mavula, President of CIRAC, delivering opening remarks at HRC61

body.text: Anselme Mavula, President of CIRAC, opened the session. He welcomed delegates and expressed appreciation to the United Nations for providing an international platform to address pressing human rights concerns.

He emphasized that such engagement remains essential to ensure that violations are neither ignored nor silenced. He highlighted the critical role of civil society in presenting ground realities and amplifying the voices of affected communities.

He stated that South Asia continues to face deep-rooted structural challenges, including unresolved conflicts, political exclusion, and limited accountability, and stressed that international forums must remain open, inclusive, and responsive.
SPEAKER: Sardar Nasir Aziz Khan — Moderator’s Intervention

body.caption: Sardar Nasir Aziz Khan, Main Representative of NGOs to the United Nations in Geneva

body.text: The discussion was moderated by Sardar Nasir Aziz Khan, Main Representative of NGOs to the United Nations in Geneva. He provided a comprehensive legal and historical framework for the discussion and reaffirmed that human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent, and interrelated, as established in Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
“Human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent, and interrelated.”

He stated that dignity, equality, and justice must guide international engagement, especially in conflict regions. He elaborated that the State of Jammu and Kashmir was established in 1846 and existed as an independent political entity until October 1947.

He explained that during the partition of the Indian subcontinent, Maharaja Hari Singh chose independence to preserve the unity of a diverse and pluralistic society. He noted that the events of 22 October 1947 resulted in violence, displacement, and the forced division of the State—leading to separation of families and denial of their right to free movement, in violation of Article 13 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

He emphasized that the Jammu and Kashmir issue is not merely territorial or bilateral but fundamentally a human issue affecting millions. He reiterated that the right to self-determination remains central under international law.

He expressed concern over increasing restrictions on civil society participation, warning that silencing independent voices undermines the integrity of international human rights mechanisms. He strongly condemned the recent assassination attempt on Dr. Farooq Abdullah, President of the Jammu Kashmir National Conference, calling it a serious security negligence and an attempt to eliminate a secular voice of Jammu and Kashmir.

He stated that it is the prime responsibility of the state to protect life, liberty, and property of people under its administration, and that terrorism or cross-border infiltration cannot be used as an excuse to evade responsibilities and international obligations.

He noted that more than one million military personnel are stationed on both sides of the ceasefire line, and it is their duty to safeguard it. He added that Jammu and Kashmir is ruled directly from the central government in New Delhi, where a Lieutenant Governor enjoys absolute powers, and even the local police is not under the jurisdiction of the Chief Minister.

He stated that India entered Kashmir through a treaty to protect the region, push back invaders, and reunite the entire State of Jammu and Kashmir. However, in 2019, India dismembered the historical State, bifurcated it, stripped Ladakh from Jammu and Kashmir, demoted statehood into two union territories, and revoked special status—actions he described as unilateral, illegal, and unacceptable to the people of Jammu and Kashmir, further aggravating a situation that could result in a potential nuclear conflict.
“There is no military solution to the Jammu and Kashmir conflict.”

He stressed that as the world’s largest democracy, India must fulfill its promises made to the people of Jammu and Kashmir. He said that democracies empower local people and uphold obligations, but instead, rights were taken away, special status revoked, and the historical State reduced to union territories.
SPEAKER: Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri

body.caption: Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri, Exiled Chairman of UKPNP

body.text: Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri, Exiled Chairman of the United Kashmir People’s National Party, delivered a detailed intervention addressing global and regional dimensions of conflict. He thanked the organizers for the opportunity to address the gathering.

He expressed deep concern over the increasingly hostile global environment, particularly the escalation involving the United States, Israel, and Iran, which he said has generated serious anxieties worldwide. He stated that conflicts of this nature rarely remain confined and often disproportionately affect vulnerable populations.

He urged the international community, especially multilateral institutions, to play a constructive role in encouraging dialogue, de-escalation, and peaceful resolution of conflicts. He highlighted concerns regarding recent political developments in Bangladesh, stating that exclusion of major political forces undermines democratic credibility.

He emphasized that democratic governance and political pluralism must be strengthened, not curtailed. Turning to Jammu and Kashmir, he stated that the issue remains one of the longest-standing unresolved matters on the UN agenda.

He said that India’s unilateral actions have fundamentally altered the historical and constitutional status of the State without the consent of its people. He noted that prolonged political restrictions have marginalized leadership, weakened institutions, and restricted meaningful participation.

He warned that such policies create deep alienation and erode confidence in democracy, rule of law, and human rights. He stated that both India and Pakistan have transformed Jammu and Kashmir into a theater of strategic rivalry and militarization, diverting resources away from human development.

He emphasized that ordinary people continue to suffer, deprived of political rights, economic opportunities, and dignity. He expressed concern over the growing communalization of politics in parts of the region, particularly India, stating that it undermines pluralism and intensifies polarization.

He highlighted that human rights violations persist across all parts of Jammu and Kashmir—whether under Indian or Pakistani administration—including shrinking civic space and restrictions on freedoms of expression, association, and peaceful assembly.

He urged the international community to support restoration of fundamental rights and meaningful political participation. He warned that escalating global tensions pose serious risks to stability and disproportionately affect vulnerable populations.
SPEAKER: Dr. Chongsi Ayeah Joseph

body.caption: Dr. Chongsi Ayeah Joseph, President and Chief Executive of CHRAPA

body.text: Dr. Chongsi Ayeah Joseph, President and Chief Executive of CHRAPA, delivered a detailed analysis of human rights challenges in South Asia. He stated that civil society professionals must present balanced assessments, unlike states that often deliver one-sided statements.

He acknowledged that South Asian states have ratified many human rights treaties, but emphasized that implementation remains weak. He highlighted that equality, non-discrimination, and participation—core principles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights—are routinely violated.

He said that religious differences and state religions create hierarchies that marginalize minorities. He noted that Article 2 of the UDHR, guaranteeing rights without discrimination, is widely violated.

He stated that when people are denied participation in governance, they become strangers in their own states. He explained that electoral calendars are manipulated, elections postponed, and political education neglected—violating Article 25 of the ICCPR.

He said that such practices undermine self-determination and deny people their identity and citizenship. He urged states to implement even one recommendation from civil society, stating that small steps can advance human rights into daily life.
SPEAKER: Fazal Rehman Afridi

body.caption: Fazal Rehman Afridi, President of IRESK

body.text: Fazal Rehman Afridi, President of IRESK, provided a detailed account of human rights violations in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and suppression of the Pashtun Tahafuz Movement (PTM). He stated that PTM, a peaceful, nonviolent grassroots movement advocating for Pashtun rights, was banned illegally by Pakistan on 6 October 2024 under the Anti-Terrorism Act of 1997.

He said the ban violates international law and Pakistan’s own constitution, and that authorities failed to provide evidence. He highlighted the case of Ali Wazir, who was released on 15 March 2026 after 1.5 years of arbitrary detention, only to be rearrested the next day on another false FIR.

He asked whether any institution in Pakistan will be held accountable for such abuses. He mentioned that other activists—including Haji Samad Khan, Hanif Pashteen, and Noor Ullah Tareen—remain imprisoned.

He stated that fundamental rights are trampled with impunity under the current hybrid regime. He highlighted the detention of former Prime Minister Imran Khan and human rights defenders such as Mahrang Baloch and Iman Mazari.

He expressed serious concern over the mysterious disappearance of PTM leader Manzoor Ahmad Pashteen since October 2024, stating that he is feared to be in the custody of Pakistani military intelligence.
SPEAKER: Mahmood Kashmiri

align.caption: Jamil Maqsood, President of the Foreign Affairs Committee of UKPNP

align.text: Jamil Maqsood, President of the Foreign Affairs Committee of UKPNP, emphasized that the situation in Jammu and Kashmir must be understood through the lens of human dignity, democratic participation, and rights. He highlighted that the region remains contested and heavily militarized, with restricted civic space.

He expressed concern over detentions of political leaders and activists in Indian-administered areas, calling for fair trials and due process. He noted similar concerns in Pakistan-administered areas, urging the release of Awami Action Committee leaders detained for peaceful activities.

He raised alarm over environmental degradation across the Himalayan region, stating that megaprojects threaten ecosystems, displace communities, and lack proper consultation. He emphasized that sustainable development must not come at the cost of environmental destruction.
“People across the region aspire to peace, dignity, and the ability to shape their future.”

He stated that people across the region aspire to peace, dignity, and the ability to shape their future. He highlighted proposals for transforming Jammu and Kashmir into a neutral, peaceful buffer promoting regional stability. He urged the international community to support dialogue, human rights monitoring, and inclusive political processes.

align.caption: Sherbaz Khan, Representative of the Awami Workers Party Gilgit-Baltistan

align.text: Sherbaz Khan, Representative of the Awami Workers Party Gilgit-Baltistan, raised concerns regarding political repression and lack of constitutional rights in Gilgit-Baltistan. He highlighted that over 2 million people face taxation without representation, despite a 1999 Supreme Court ruling.

He stated that military-linked institutions increasingly control economic infrastructure, including the takeover of Sost Dry Port. He raised concerns over the Land Reforms Act 2025, which allows transfer of ancestral lands to military and federal entities—described by locals as land dispossession.

He noted that activists have been detained under anti-terror laws and that the killing of political figure Javed Naji requires independent investigation. He highlighted environmental damage from megaprojects such as the Diamer-Bhasha Dam, which displaced thousands without adequate compensation.

He criticized the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC) for lacking transparency and enabling exploitation of natural resources without community consent. He called on the international community to recognize Gilgit-Baltistan as a disputed territory lacking constitutional rights, halt land dispossession, ensure accountability, release political prisoners, and protect environmental rights.

Throughout the discussion, participants emphasized that the people of Jammu and Kashmir continue to face denial of fundamental rights, including freedom of movement, democratic participation, and access to justice. They highlighted concerns regarding arbitrary detention, suppression of civil liberties, environmental degradation, and lack of accountability.

Participants called upon the international community, particularly the UN Human Rights Council, to strengthen monitoring mechanisms, ensure civil society participation, promote dialogue, and uphold international human rights standards.
“Human rights are non-negotiable, and the people of Jammu and Kashmir must be allowed to live with dignity, freedom, and justice.”

In his concluding remarks, Sardar Nasir Aziz Khan stated that there is no military solution to the Jammu and Kashmir conflict. He said the issue must be resolved peacefully in accordance with UN resolutions and the wishes of the people.

He urged India and Pakistan to fulfill their promises and international obligations. He called on Pakistan and local authorities to honor commitments made with the Joint Awami Action Committee and to restrain from using force against peaceful rights movements in Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan.

He also urged the Joint Awami Action Committee to continue dialogue and negotiations as the only way to secure rights and protect lives. He urged India to honor the resolution passed by the Jammu Kashmir Assembly demanding restoration of special status and statehood of the historical State of Jammu and Kashmir, including Ladakh as its historical part.

The participants reaffirmed that human rights are non-negotiable and that the people of the historical State of Jammu and Kashmir must be allowed to live with dignity, freedom, justice, right to free movement and the right to determine their future.
